candidates.attacker_control: The URL string passed to XSSAPI.getValidHref(String), XSSFilter.isValidHref(String) (e.g. a request parameter / stored content value that an application feeds into these validators before rendering an or attribute). No authentication, configuration or repository write access is required.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Checked that the code DOES attempt entity normalization (unescapeXml) and that XSSFilterImpl.isValidHref re-decodes and re-validates a second time - so a simple percent-encoded or numeric-entity payload ('%6a%61...',':') is rejected; the existing test XSSFilterImplTest.isValidHref (lines 51-57) covers exactly those two forms and is consistent with the source, which is why I did not report them. Verified that the allow-list regexps really do admit '&' and ';' (DEFAULT_HREF_ATTRIBUTE lines 75-76; config.xml line 70) so the entity-carrying payload is not filtered earlier, and that no output-encoding step in getValidHref would remove the ':' sequence. Also considered whether the value is ever HTML-escaped on output: the API returns the raw entity-carrying string and the javadoc states it is meant for attribute insertion, so no further escaping is implied.
candidates.impact: Client-side script execution in the context of the victim's session when an application relies on XSSAPI.getValidHref/XSSFilter.isValidHref as its XSS defense for URLs (session/credential theft, CSRF-token theft, defacement, actions as the victim). It also undermines the filter's own defense-in-depth because the same allow-list governs AntiSamy 'onsiteURL'/'offsiteURL' attribute validation in config.xml. Availability/robustness side effects are not part of this claim.
candidates.prerequisites: A consuming application uses the sanitizer output directly as an HTML attribute value (the documented use: 'Sanitizes a URL for writing as an HTML href or src attribute value') and the browser decodes HTML named character references in attribute values (normal HTML5 parsing). The payload must contain no literal ':' outside a scheme prefix and no characters rejected by the allow-list; the shipped policy's onsiteURL regexp and the hardcoded DEFAULT_HREF_ATTRIBUTE both permit '&' and ';'.
candidates.root_cause: The sanitizer normalizes attacker input for validation using percent-decoding (URLDecoder.decode) plus XML-entity decoding (StringEscapeUtils.unescapeXml, which only handles amp/lt/gt/quot/apos and numeric references). It never applies HTML named-character-reference decoding, although the sanitized result is documented and intended to be written into an HTML attribute (XSSAPI.getValidHref javadoc; XSSFilter.isValidHref javadoc). The allowed-href regexps in XSSFilterImpl.DEFAULT_HREF_ATTRIBUTE (lines 75-76) and in the shipped AntiSamy policy (config.xml 'onsiteURL' regexp, line 70) accept '&' and ';' as ordinary URL characters, so a string carrying the named entity ':' contains no literal ':' and matches the allow-list. The sanitizer then returns that string unchanged, and the browser decodes the entity into ':' while parsing the attribute value, reconstructing 'javascript:' (validated value != value that is finally interpreted).
candidates.title: getValidHref/isValidHref href sanitizer can be bypassed with HTML named character references (:), yielding javascript: URLs
candidates.trace: 1) XSSAPIImpl.getValidHref(url): URLDecoder.decode(url, UTF-8) (line 232) -> StringEscapeUtils.unescapeXml(...) (line 237) -> percent-encoding of only " ' > < ` and space (lines 241-246) -> ':' rewriting limited to the query string when '?' is present (lines 247-250) -> mangleNamespaces (line 252) -> xssFilter.isValidHref(encodedUrl) (line 253). 2) For input 'javascript:alert(1)': there are no '%' escapes, and unescapeXml does not recognize the HTML named reference ':' (XML predefined entities only), so the literal characters remain 'javascript:alert(1)'. No '?' is present, so the colon-rewriting branch is skipped; mangleNamespaces finds no ':' and no '://', so the value is unchanged. 3) XSSFilterImpl.isValidHref(encodedUrl) (lines 127-146) then decodes again; because no '%' and no XML entity is present, the guard 'xmlDecodedURL.equals(url) || xmlDecodedURL.equals(decodedURL)' is true and runHrefValidation(url) (line 150-153) evaluates the string as-is. 4) runHrefValidation uses the policy href Attribute: containsAllowedValue(...) is false (allowedValues is empty for the shipped policy) and matchesAllowedExpression(...) applies the onsiteURL pattern [\p{L}\p{M}*+\p{N}\\.\#@\$%\+&;\-_~,\?=/!\*\(\)]* which accepts letters, '&', ';', digits, '(' and ')'; the whole payload matches, so isValidHref returns true. 5) getValidHref returns the entity-carrying string unmodified; when it is emitted inside an HTML attribute the browser decodes ':' to ':' and resolves a 'javascript:' URL.
candidates.unverified: Not runtime-confirmed: I could not execute code, run the tests, or query a browser/HTML parser in this environment, and the entity table of org.apache.commons.lang3.StringEscapeUtils 3.6 (a provided dependency, not present in the snapshot) was not inspected directly - the claim that ':' survives unescapeXml is based on the documented XML-predefined-entity scope of that helper. I also could not confirm in-repo which historical fix corresponds to this snapshot, and no test in the snapshot exercises HTML named character references (the unused test resource src/test/resources/configWithoutHref.xml shows the href allow-list has been a moving target, but does not cover this case). No end-to-end consumer of getValidHref exists in this repository, so the real-world impact depends on downstream applications inserting the result into an HTML attribute.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-79 Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation (XSS) / CWE-180-ish encoding mismatch: HTML-entity decoding not applied before URL-scheme validation

coverage_summary: Scope: 19 of 20 files in the assigned tree are model-visible (one file is withheld by the sensitive-name/path filter, so its content was not reviewed); 13 Java files, pom.xml, README, ESAPI.properties, validation.properties, src/main/resources/SLING-INF/content/config.xml and src/test/resources/configWithoutHref.xml were read or searched. All main Java classes (XSSAPIImpl, XSSFilterImpl, XSSFilterRule, HtmlToHtmlContentContext, PlainTextToHtmlContentContext, PolicyHandler, LongValidationRule, ProtectionContext, XSSAPI, XSSFilter) and both test classes were inspected with line-level reading. P1 index coverage is partial: only syntax-level symbols/containment plus name-based call and inheritance candidates (150 symbols, 260 calls, 225 edges, 205 unresolved calls); control flow, data flow and semantic resolution are unimplemented, and OSGi/Spring annotation wiring, runtime DI and security enforcement are explicitly unverified. XML/properties resources were searched by text; the AntiSamy policy was only sampled (regexps and anchor/link/img tags), not exhaustively reviewed.
limitations: No code execution, tests, scanners or exploit payloads were run; all statements are static source reasoning and the candidate is a lead, not a confirmed vulnerability.
One repository file is excluded from view by the source safety filter; its content could not be considered.

The P1 index provides only syntactic/navigation candidates (no control flow, data flow, semantic resolution, reachability or exploitability proof), so call/reference completeness is not guaranteed (205 unresolved calls).

Externals not in the snapshot (commons-lang3 3.6 entity tables, AntiSamy 1.5.2 policy/lookup semantics, OWASP Java Encoder 1.1.1 behavior, browser HTML entity decoding) were reasoned about from documentation-level knowledge, not verified from source or runtime.
The AntiSamy policy config.xml has ~2800 lines; only the regexps and href/src/action attributes and anchor/link/script-related tags were sampled, so other allow-list weaknesses may exist unexamined.
No in-repository consumer of XSSAPI.getValidHref/XSSFilter.isValidHref is present, so end-to-end exploitability depends on downstream applications and remains unverified.

rejected_leads.lead: Unhandled IllegalArgumentException in getValidHref/isValidHref for malformed percent-escapes (e.g. "%", "%zz"): both methods only catch UnsupportedEncodingException around URLDecoder.decode (XSSAPIImpl.java lines 231-258; XSSFilterImpl.java lines 131-145), so attacker-supplied URLs can raise a runtime exception (500 responses / request-path DoS).
rejected_leads.reason: Real robustness defect with only availability impact and no evidence of the security boundary being crossed; kept out of the single candidate slot, which is reserved for the XSS-impact lead.

rejected_leads.lead: XSSAPIImpl.mangleNamespaces (lines 186-222) passes attacker-influenced group-1 text into Matcher.appendReplacement without Matcher.quoteReplacement, so '$' or '\' sequences in a crafted path can raise IllegalArgumentException or corrupt the mangled output.
rejected_leads.reason: Same availability class as above; the output corruption path (interpreting '$1' in the replacement) was not shown to weaken validation in a way that yields script execution.

rejected_leads.lead: XSSFilterImpl.isValidHref validates the still-percent-encoded form when decoding succeeded (lines 138-141), so isValidHref("%6a%61%76%61%73%63%72%69%70%74%3aalert(1)") returns true.
rejected_leads.reason: Exploitation would require a downstream component to percent-decode the value again after validation; browsers do not percent-decode an href before scheme resolution, so no XSS path could be established from source alone. Unconfirmed and excluded from the candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: updateDefaultHandler sets the default handler to null and rebuilds it while filter()/check() read the field unsynchronized, and the default policy is loaded from repository content via the sling/xss/config.xml search path (XSSFilterImpl.java lines 216-257, 168-191).
rejected_leads.reason: Requires concurrent policy reload for a possible NPE (DoS) and, for policy substitution, repository write access to the searched paths - an administrative/config assumption rather than attacker-controlled input in this code.

rejected_leads.lead: Shipped AntiSamy policy (src/main/resources/SLING-INF/content/config.xml) permits attributes such as target/name/onFocus/onBlur on the anchor tag and may carry permissive regexps.
rejected_leads.reason: The relevant URL regexps (onsiteURL/offsiteURL) do reject a literal ':' scheme, so no concrete policy-level bypass was demonstrated; this remains an uninspected-largely allow-list, not a finding.

summary: Reviewed the Apache Sling XSS Protection bundle (org.apache.sling.xss, 2.0.3-SNAPSHOT): 19 of 20 files visible (one file excluded by the safety filter), 13 Java sources parsed by the relation index, XML/properties/pom resources inspected directly. The strongest source-evidenced lead is in the URL-sanitization path: the API decodes XML/numeric entities before validating a candidate `href`/`src` value, but validates the *validated* form against regexps that permit `&` and `;`, while the value is later consumed by an HTML parser that also decodes HTML named character references (e.g. `:`) that `StringEscapeUtils.unescapeXml` does not touch. A payload such as `javascript:alert(1)` therefore contains no literal colon during validation, matches the allowed href regexp, and is returned unchanged — to be decoded by the browser into an executable `javascript:` URL. This is a plausible XSS-filter bypass (CWE-79) in a security API whose documented contract is to sanitize values for `href`/`src` attributes. It is a lead, not a runtime-confirmed vulnerability. Several weaker availability/robustness leads were found but rejected or left unconfirmed (uncaught IllegalArgumentException from URLDecoder on malformed `%` input, unquoted `Matcher.appendReplacement` in mangleNamespaces, non-atomic default-policy reload, and a decode-consistency asymmetry in isValidHref).
